before.content_html:
What Is Creative iMedia?

The OCR Cambridge National in Creative iMedia is a vocational qualification designed to give you knowledge and skills used in the media industry. It covers how media products are planned, designed, and produced — from websites and animations to films and digital games.

The qualification is made up of three units: one externally assessed exam (R093) and two centre-assessed NEA units. The R093 exam is the focus of your revision — it is worth 40% of the overall qualification and tests your knowledge and understanding of the media industry, product design, pre-production planning, and distribution.

Key Fact

The R093 exam is 1 hour 30 minutes, worth 70 marks in total. Section A has 10 marks (short answer and multiple choice). Section B has 60 marks (context-based questions including three extended responses).

The Four Topic Areas of R093

The R093 exam covers four topic areas that you must revise thoroughly. Each topic area will have at least one question in both Section A and Section B of the exam.

Topic Area 1: The Media Industry — covers the different sectors (traditional and new media), types of media products, and the job roles involved in creating them. Topic Area 2: Factors Influencing Product Design — covers purpose, style, content, layout, client requirements, audience demographics, research methods, and media codes. Topic Area 3: Pre-production Planning — covers work plans, planning documents (mind maps, mood boards, storyboards, scripts, wireframes), legal issues, regulation, and health and safety. Topic Area 4: Distribution Considerations — covers distribution platforms, file properties, and file formats for images, audio, and moving image.

Section A uses 7–10 closed response, multiple choice, and short answer questions that test recall of knowledge and understanding. Section B presents a short scenario that develops through the paper. You apply your knowledge to produce relevant responses. Section B includes short answer questions and three extended response questions — two that assess analysis and evaluation, and one that assesses recall and application of knowledge.

What Is the Media Industry?

The media industry is vast. It covers both traditional media and new media sectors and provides work for individual freelance creatives as well as large teams in design houses and multinational companies.

The industry produces a wide range of products — from films and TV programmes to websites, digital games, animations, and social media content. Job roles frequently overlap multiple sectors, and products often need to be suitable for more than one kind of output. Despite this variety, there are common aspects to all media products: pre-production and planning are vital, and media codes are used to convey meaning, create impact, and engage audiences.

Key Fact

The media industry is divided into traditional media (film, television, radio, print publishing) and new media (computer games, interactive media, internet, digital publishing). New media is digital and still evolving.

Performance Objectives in the Exam

The R093 exam assesses three Performance Objectives (POs). PO1: Recall knowledge and show understanding — this means being able to identify, define, and recall facts. PO2: Apply knowledge and understanding — this means using what you know to answer questions about specific scenarios. PO3: Analyse and evaluate knowledge, understanding and performance — this means weighing up options, discussing advantages and disadvantages, and making justified conclusions.

Identify — select the relevant part or state what it is. Describe — use words to express a concept so it is clear for the reader. Explain — include reasons why, using the word “because”. Discuss — give both sides of the argument with analysis and evaluation. Outline — state the key points with a brief description.

Understanding these command words is essential. If a question says “identify”, a single word or short phrase is enough. If it says “discuss”, you need to explore both sides and reach a conclusion. Misreading the command word is one of the most common reasons students lose marks.

Key Fact

The exam always includes context-based questions in Section B. You will be given a scenario about a media company or project and must apply your knowledge to that specific context — generic answers without reference to the scenario will score lower marks.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Creative iMedia J834 has one exam unit (R093) worth 40% of the qualification, covering four topic areas: the media industry, factors influencing product design, pre-production planning, and distribution considerations.
  • The media industry spans traditional media (film, TV, radio, print) and new media (games, interactive media, internet, digital publishing) with many overlapping job roles and products.
  • Understanding exam command words (identify, describe, explain, discuss) is critical for maximising your marks in the R093 paper.

practice_questions.text: A media company wants to create a promotional campaign for a new energy drink aimed at 16-25 year olds. Describe the types of media sectors they could use and explain why.

Lower band (1-2): Limited identification of sectors.

• New media such as internet/social media — young audience is digitally native, use platforms like Instagram/TikTok

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether traditional media or new media is more effective for reaching a young audience. In your answer you should consider both types of media.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion of both types with analysis and a justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with analysis of both sides.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some discussion with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little development.
Indicative content:
New media advantages:
• Young people spend more time online / on social media
• Can target specific demographics
• Cheaper and more flexible, can be updated quickly
• Interactive engagement possible
Traditional media advantages:
• Still has wide reach (TV, cinema)
• Can create high-impact advertising (film trailers, TV spots)
• Some young people still consume traditional media
Conclusion should weigh both sides and justify which is more effective for the specific audience.

before.content_html:
Understanding Media Sectors

The media sector is a distinct area of the media industry. The OCR specification divides the media industry into two broad categories: traditional media and new media. You need to know the sectors within each category, understand how they differ, and recognise that the industry is constantly evolving as technology advances.

Key Fact

Traditional media sectors: film, television, radio, print publishing. New media sectors: computer games, interactive media, internet, digital publishing.

Traditional Media Sectors

Traditional media refers to non-digital media channels that have been around for decades. These are well-established channels of communication that reach large audiences.

Film — the film industry produces movies for cinema and home viewing. Films are created by large teams including directors, camera operators, editors, and actors. Films have large budgets and can take years to produce, but reach global audiences. Television — TV broadcasts programmes including dramas, documentaries, news, and entertainment shows. TV reaches mass audiences through scheduled broadcasting and, increasingly, on-demand streaming. Radio — radio broadcasts audio content including music, talk shows, news, and drama. It is one of the oldest forms of mass media and remains popular for its accessibility. Print publishing — this covers newspapers, magazines, books, comics, and leaflets. Print was historically the main way information was shared with large audiences.

Advantages: traditional media targets a wide “mass” audience, has established credibility and trust, and produces high-quality, polished content. Disadvantages: it can be hard to target a specific group of consumers, traditional media often requires a large budget, channels like film and TV can take a long time to develop, and content cannot be quickly adapted to respond to changes in the wider world.

New Media Sectors

New media refers to digital media channels that have arrived more recently and are still evolving. These channels use digital technology to create and distribute content.

Computer games — the gaming industry creates interactive entertainment for consoles, PCs, and mobile devices. It is now one of the largest entertainment sectors globally. Interactive media — this includes any digital product that responds to user input, such as interactive websites, touchscreen kiosks, and VR/AR experiences. Internet — the internet is a platform for websites, streaming services, social media, blogs, and online advertising. It allows content to reach global audiences instantly. Digital publishing — this covers eBooks, online magazines, digital newspapers, podcasts, and web graphics. Digital publishing allows content to be distributed without physical printing costs.

Advantages: new media can target much more specific audiences of consumers, it can be much cheaper to produce and distribute, channels can be updated quickly (minute by minute), making them cheap, flexible, and adaptable, and audiences expect the most up-to-date content. Disadvantages: there is high competition for attention online, content can be easily copied or pirated, audiences may distrust unregulated content, and technology can become outdated quickly.

How Media Sectors Are Evolving

The media industry does not stand still. Traditional and new media are increasingly converging — meaning they are merging together. A newspaper might have a print edition (traditional) and a website with video content (new media). A TV show might be broadcast live (traditional) and also streamed online (new media). Radio stations now podcast their shows for on-demand listening.

The specification states you must know that media sectors are evolving. This evolution is driven by technology — faster internet speeds, smartphones, and social media platforms have changed how audiences consume content. Streaming services like Netflix and Disney+ have disrupted traditional TV and film distribution. Social media platforms allow anyone to become a content creator, blurring the line between producers and consumers.

Key Fact

The same product can be used by different sectors. For example, a video could be used in film (cinema), television (broadcast), the internet (streaming/social media), and interactive media (embedded in a website). This cross-sector use is a key concept in the R093 exam.

A daily newspaper available online and in print uses both print publishing and internet sectors. A TV channel that streams from its website uses television and internet. A radio show available as a podcast uses radio and digital publishing. A new book released on Amazon Kindle uses print publishing and digital publishing. These examples show how modern media products rarely belong to just one sector.

Conclusion: Both have their place; most campaigns use a combination.

before.content_html:
Types of Media Products

The media industry produces a wide range of different media products. You need to know what these products are, how they are used, and which sectors produce them. The R093 specification lists thirteen types of product that you must be able to identify and describe. Importantly, the same product can be used by different sectors.

Key Fact

The 13 media products you must know: video, audio, music, animation, special effects (SFX/VFX), digital imaging and graphics, social media platforms/apps, digital games, comics and graphic novels, websites, multimedia, eBooks, AR/VR.

Audio-Visual Products

Video includes any moving image content such as films, TV programmes, online videos, and advertisements. Video is used across multiple sectors including film, television, internet, and interactive media. Audio covers sound-based content including radio broadcasts, podcasts, sound effects, and voiceovers. Audio is used in radio, internet, film, and digital publishing. Music is a specific type of audio product created for entertainment, advertising, or to accompany other media. Music is used in film, television, radio, computer games, and internet platforms.

Animation involves creating the illusion of movement using a sequence of images. There are several types of animation you should know: traditional/cel animation, 2D animation, 3D animation, motion graphics animation, and stop motion animation. Animation is used in film, television, computer games, internet, and interactive media.

Traditional/cel animation — each frame is drawn by hand on transparent sheets. Disney’s early films like Snow White used this technique. 2D animation — digital drawing on a flat plane, used in cartoons and explainer videos. 3D animation — computer-generated models that exist in three dimensions, used in films like Toy Story and modern video games. Motion graphics — animated graphic design elements like moving text, logos, and infographics. Stop motion — physical objects are moved in small increments between individual photographs, creating movement when played in sequence. Wallace and Gromit is a well-known example.

Special Effects: SFX and VFX

There is an important distinction between SFX (special effects) and VFX (visual effects). SFX are physical effects created during production on set — examples include make-up, prosthetics, pyrotechnics/explosions, live weather effects, and animatronics. VFX are digital effects added after production using CGI — examples include digital explosions, virtual backdrops, monsters/animals, and magic/superpowers.

Key Fact

SFX = physical effects created during production (on set). VFX = digital effects added after production (in post-production using CGI). Both are used in film, TV, and computer games.

Digital and Interactive Products

Digital imaging and graphics covers photographs, illustrations, logos, and graphic designs created or edited digitally. A bitmap/raster graphic is a digital image composed of pixels. Graphics are used across virtually all media sectors. Social media platforms/apps are online services that allow users to create and share content, such as Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube. Digital games are interactive entertainment played on consoles, PCs, or mobile devices. Comics and graphic novels combine illustrations and text to tell stories — they can be physical or digital.

Websites are collections of web pages accessed through browsers, used for information, e-commerce, entertainment, and communication. Multimedia products combine multiple types of media (text, images, audio, video, animation) in a single product, such as an interactive presentation or educational app. eBooks are digital versions of books that can be read on devices like Kindle or tablets.

Augmented Reality (AR) combines computer-generated images with the real-world environment on a screen. The user sees the physical world with digital elements overlaid on top. Examples include Pokémon Go, Snapchat filters, and Google search AR features. Virtual Reality (VR) is a fully immersive computer-simulated environment that replaces the user’s real-world surroundings. The user wears a headset and experiences a completely digital world. Examples include VR gaming, virtual tours, and training simulations. Both AR and VR are used in film, computer games, and interactive media.

Products Across Sectors

A critical concept for the exam is that the same product can be used by different sectors. Video is used in film (cinema), television (broadcast), internet (streaming and social media), and interactive media (embedded in websites). Audio is used in radio (broadcast), internet (podcasts), and film (soundtracks). Understanding which products belong to which sectors — and that many products cross sector boundaries — is essential for the R093 exam.

Key Fact

The exam will often ask you to match products to sectors or explain why a particular product is suitable for a specific sector. Always think about the purpose of the product and the audience it is trying to reach.

practice_questions.text: A company is creating an educational product about space for children aged 8-12. Describe three types of media products that could be used and explain why each would be suitable.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (5-6): Three products clearly described with explanations linked to the educational context and audience.
Mid band (3-4): Two products with some explanation.
Lower band (1-2): Limited identification.
Indicative content:
• Animation — visually engaging for children, can explain complex concepts simply
• AR/VR — immersive experience to explore planets/space, engaging for young learners
• Digital games — interactive learning through play, appeals to the age group
• Website/multimedia — combines text, images, video for comprehensive learning
• eBook — accessible on tablets, can include interactive elements

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using VFX rather than SFX in a film production.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion of both VFX and SFX with analysis and a justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with analysis of both sides.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some discussion with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little development.
Indicative content:
VFX advantages:
• Can create effects impossible to achieve physically (e.g. dragons, space)
• Safer — no risk of injury from pyrotechnics
• Can be edited and refined after filming
• Can be more cost-effective for large-scale effects
VFX disadvantages:
• Requires expensive software and skilled artists
• Can look unrealistic if poorly done
• Time-consuming post-production process
SFX advantages:
• Look more realistic and tangible on screen
• Actors can react to physical effects naturally
Conclusion: Most modern films use a combination of both.

lessons.title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 1)

before.content_html:
Job Roles in the Media Industry

The media industry employs people in a wide range of job roles. The OCR specification organises these into three categories: creative roles, technical roles, and senior roles. You need to know the main responsibilities of each role, how each contributes to creating media products, and which production phases each role is specific to.

Key Fact

There are four production phases: pre-production (planning, research, design), production (creating/filming/recording), post-production (editing, adding effects, refining), and distribution (delivering the finished product to audiences).

Creative Roles

Creative roles are responsible for the artistic and design elements of media products. These professionals bring ideas to life through visual design, writing, and artistic skills.

Animator — creates animation sequences using traditional, 2D, 3D, or stop motion techniques. Works across pre-production (research, drafts, storyboarding), production (creating animation), and post-production (refining). Content creator — produces digital content for platforms such as social media, websites, and blogs. May work across all production phases. Copywriter — writes engaging text for advertisements, websites, scripts, and marketing materials. Primarily works in pre-production and production. Graphic designer — creates visual content including logos, layouts, posters, and digital graphics. Works mainly in pre-production (design concepts) and production (creating final designs).

Illustrator/graphic artist — creates original drawings and illustrations for print and digital media, including book illustrations, comic art, and concept art. Photographer — captures still images for use in advertising, publishing, journalism, and digital media. Primarily works during production. Script writer — writes scripts for films, TV programmes, radio shows, and other media. Script writers work specifically in pre-production — their work must be completed before production can begin. Web designer — designs the visual layout and user experience of websites, considering colour, typography, navigation, and content placement.

Pre-production only: script writer. Pre-production and production: copywriter, graphic designer, illustrator, web designer. All phases: animator (researches, creates, refines), content creator (plans, creates, edits, publishes). Production only: photographer. Some creative roles span multiple phases because they contribute to planning, creating, and refining the product.

Technical Roles

Technical roles focus on the equipment, technology, and technical processes needed to produce and edit media content.

Camera operator — operates camera equipment during filming, understanding shot types, angles, and movement. Works primarily during production but liaises with the client and director in pre-production to plan shots. Games programmer/developer — writes the code that makes digital games function, including gameplay mechanics, graphics rendering, and user interfaces. Works mainly in production and post-production. Sound editor — edits and mixes audio tracks after recording, adding sound effects and balancing levels. Works in post-production. Audio technician — operates sound recording equipment during production, ensuring high-quality audio capture. Works during production.

Video editor — assembles and edits recorded video footage in post-production, cutting scenes, adding transitions, and creating the final sequence. Web developer — builds and codes websites using programming languages, turning the web designer’s visual plans into functional sites. Works mainly in production.

Pre-production tasks: mind maps, mood boards, visualisation diagrams, storyboards, script writing, designing client briefs, identifying timescales, carrying out research, producing work plans, identifying target audience, identifying equipment needs, considering health and safety, considering legislation. Production tasks: filming, sound recording, creating media graphics, recording music/soundtracks, creating websites, creating animations. Post-production tasks: editing, adding CGI, adding sound effects, adding opening/closing titles and credits, editing music. Distribution: changing formats to meet client needs.

Key Fact

Some job roles are specific to one production phase (e.g. script writer — pre-production only). Some span multiple phases (e.g. animator works across pre-production, production, and post-production). The size and scale of a project may mean one individual performs more than one role.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Creative roles (animator, content creator, copywriter, graphic designer, illustrator, photographer, script writer, web designer) focus on artistic and design elements of media products.
  • Technical roles (camera operator, games programmer, sound editor, audio technician, video editor, web developer) focus on equipment, technology, and technical processes.
  • Each role contributes to specific production phases (pre-production, production, post-production, distribution), though some roles span multiple phases and individuals may perform more than one role on smaller projects.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a graphic designer could contribute to a promotional campaign for a new product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• A graphic designer creates visual content such as logos, posters, and digital graphics (1). They would design eye-catching promotional materials that communicate the brand’s message (1). practice_questions.text: A small independent film company is producing a short film with a limited budget. Describe how the size of the team might affect how job roles are allocated.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation of how limited budget affects role allocation with specific examples.
Mid band (3-4): Some understanding with basic examples.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points.
Indicative content:
• Individuals may perform more than one role (e.g. camera operator also acts as video editor and sound editor)
• Creative and technical roles may be combined (e.g. director also writes the script)
• Fewer specialist roles available — generalists needed
• Budget constraints mean they cannot hire separate people for each role
• In larger productions, each role would be performed by a specialist
• Quality may be affected if one person tries to do too many tasks

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of the pre-production phase in creating a successful media product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion with analysis of benefits and potential drawbacks of extensive pre-production.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some discussion with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points.
Indicative content:
Importance of pre-production:
• Planning saves time and money during production
• Storyboards/scripts ensure the team has a clear vision
• Research identifies target audience needs
• Risk assessments ensure health and safety
• Work plans keep the project on schedule
• Client briefs are agreed before production starts
Counterpoints:
• Spending too long on pre-production can delay the project
• Plans may need to change during production anyway
• Over-planning can stifle creativity
Conclusion: Pre-production is essential for professional, well-organised media products.

lessons.title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 2)

before.content_html:
Senior Roles in the Media Industry

Senior roles in the media industry involve managing teams, overseeing projects, and making high-level creative and strategic decisions. These professionals ensure that media products are completed on time, on budget, and to the required quality. The OCR specification identifies five senior roles you must know.

Campaign manager — plans and oversees marketing or advertising campaigns from start to finish. They coordinate the team, set timescales, manage budgets, and ensure the campaign meets the client’s objectives. A campaign manager works across all production phases. Creative director — leads the creative vision of a project or organisation. They make decisions about the overall look, feel, and message of media products, ensuring consistency across all outputs. They work closely with designers, copywriters, and other creative roles.

Director — the creative lead of a film, TV programme, or other moving image production. The director holds the creative vision throughout the entire process, from pre-production through to the final edit. They work with the script writer, appoint heads of department, select actors with casting directors, choreograph scenes (“blocking”), instruct crew on lighting, wardrobe, and make-up, and lead the editing of the final cut. Editor — a senior role that oversees the editorial direction of content, particularly in publishing and journalism. In film/TV, the editor makes creative decisions about how footage is assembled. Production manager — manages the practical and logistical aspects of a production across all stages. They coordinate schedules, budgets, crew, equipment, and locations.

Key Fact

A production manager manages all stages of production. They are responsible for the practical logistics, not the creative decisions. A director holds the creative vision and makes artistic decisions. Both roles span multiple production phases.

How Roles Contribute to Media Products

Every role in the media industry contributes to the final product in a specific way. The exam may ask you to explain how a particular role contributes to a given scenario. To answer well, you need to connect the role’s responsibilities to the specific media product being discussed.

In pre-production, the script writer creates the screenplay, the director develops the creative vision, the production manager organises the schedule and budget, and the graphic designer creates concept art. In production, the camera operator films scenes under the director’s guidance, the audio technician records sound, the photographer captures promotional stills, and actors perform. In post-production, the video editor assembles the footage, the sound editor mixes audio, VFX artists add digital effects, and the director oversees the final cut. In distribution, the finished product is converted into appropriate formats and released to audiences through cinemas, streaming platforms, or broadcasts.

Freelance vs Employed Work

People in the media industry can work as either freelance workers or as permanent employees. Many creative and technical professionals in the media industry work freelance, taking on projects for different clients. This is especially common for roles like photographers, animators, graphic designers, and web developers.

Freelance advantages: flexibility to choose projects and working hours, ability to work for multiple clients, potential to earn more by setting own rates, variety of work across different sectors. Freelance disadvantages: no guaranteed income or job security, must manage own tax, insurance, and business expenses, no paid holiday or sick leave, must constantly find new clients.

Employed advantages: regular salary and job security, paid holiday, sick pay, and pension contributions, training and career development provided by employer, clear career progression pathway. Employed disadvantages: less flexibility over working hours and projects, may earn less than successful freelancers, limited variety of work, may need to follow company creative direction rather than own vision.

Key Fact

The size and scale of a project affects how roles are allocated. In a large production, each role is performed by a specialist. In a small project, one person may perform multiple roles (e.g. a camera operator might also edit the video and mix the sound).

Career Paths in the Media Industry

The media industry offers many career paths. Creative iMedia provides a foundation for further study and work in media-related fields. Progression routes from this qualification include A Level Media Studies, Cambridge Technicals in Digital Media and Information Technology (Level 2 or 3), T Level qualifications in Digital Production Design and Development or Media, Broadcast and Production, and apprenticeships such as the Media and Broadcast Assistant Pathway.

A person interested in film might start as a runner (assisting on set), progress to camera operator or assistant director, and eventually become a director or production manager. A web designer might start as a junior designer, learn coding to become a web developer, and eventually become a creative director at a digital agency. A content creator might start with a personal social media channel and progress to working for a marketing agency as a campaign manager. The transferable skills developed in Creative iMedia — creative thinking, digital presentation, planning, and problem solving — are valuable across many industries.

The specification identifies several transferable skills that Creative iMedia develops: creative thinking and innovation, analytical and critical thinking, digital presentation skills, project planning and time management, problem solving, and teamwork. These skills are useful not just in the media industry but in any career.

practice_questions.text: A local charity wants to create a short promotional video to raise awareness of their work. Describe how three different job roles would contribute to the production of this video.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (5-6): Three roles clearly described with specific contributions linked to the charity video scenario.
Mid band (3-4): Two roles with some explanation.
Lower band (1-2): Limited identification.
Indicative content:
• Script writer — writes the script/narrative for the video, planning what message to communicate about the charity
• Camera operator — films the footage, choosing appropriate shots and angles to capture the charity’s work
• Video editor — assembles and edits the footage in post-production, adding titles and transitions
• Director — oversees the creative vision, ensuring the video effectively communicates the charity’s message
• Graphic designer — creates any graphics, titles, or branding elements for the video

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether it is better for a media company to employ permanent staff or hire freelancers for a large advertising campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks using a best-fit approach:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion of both options with analysis and a justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some discussion with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points.
Indicative content:
Permanent staff:
• Already know the company’s brand and values
• Available immediately, no recruitment delay
• Consistent quality and communication
• More expensive long-term (salaries, benefits)
Freelancers:
• Specialist skills for specific tasks (e.g. hiring a VFX specialist)
• Only paid for the project — can be more cost-effective
• Fresh perspective and new ideas
• Less control over quality and availability
• May not understand the brand as well
Conclusion: A combination is often best — permanent staff for core work, freelancers for specialist tasks.
